content.value_statement: Multiplayer games need clear networking decisions before implementation starts. This skill guides architecture, synchronization, latency, security, and matchmaking tradeoffs.
actual_capabilities: Compare dedicated server, peer-to-peer, host-based, turn-based, and distributed multiplayer architectures.
Explain state synchronization, input synchronization, hybrid sync, prediction, interpolation, and reconciliation choices.
Suggest bandwidth reduction methods such as delta compression, quantization, prioritization, and area-of-interest filtering.
Outline server-authoritative validation and anti-cheat principles for movement, inventory, visibility, and hit detection.
Identify matchmaking factors such as skill, latency, wait time, and party size.
limitations: It provides planning guidance, not a complete multiplayer framework.
It does not include engine-specific implementation code.
It does not run load tests or measure live network performance.
It does not replace expert security review for competitive games.

use_cases.title: Choose a Network Model
use_cases.description: Select a practical multiplayer architecture for a new game based on pace, scale, fairness, and operating cost.

use_cases.title: Review Synchronization Design
use_cases.description: Evaluate prediction, interpolation, reconciliation, and update rates before a prototype reaches production scope.

use_cases.title: Plan Anti-Cheat Controls

prompt_templates.title: Pick an Architecture
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner planning for a new multiplayer game.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Sync Strategies
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate design review for gameplay synchronization.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the multiplayer skill to compare state sync, input sync, and hybrid sync for my game. Recommend one approach and explain why.

prompt_templates.title: Design Latency Handling
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced planning for responsive real-time play.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the multiplayer skill to design prediction, interpolation, reconciliation, and lag compensation for this gameplay loop.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Multiplayer Security
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the multiplayer skill to review my multiplayer design for trust boundaries, anti-cheat controls, hidden data exposure, and server validation gaps.

output_examples.input: I am building a four-player cooperative action game with low budget hosting.
output_examples.output: Recommended architecture: host-based with server-authoritative rules where possible. Use prediction for local movement, interpolation for remote players, and server checks for inventory and damage.

output_examples.input: I need to reduce bandwidth for a large arena match.
output: Send delta updates instead of full state snapshots.
Prioritize nearby entities and urgent combat events.
Reduce precision for positions, rotations, and non-critical values.

output_examples.input: I want to prevent common client cheats in a competitive shooter.
output_examples.output: Make the server authoritative for movement, inventory, visibility, and hit validation. Never trust client claims without timing, line-of-sight, and state checks.

best_practices: Start with the gameplay model, then choose the network architecture that fits fairness, latency, scale, and cost.
Keep the server authoritative for important game state, especially combat, inventory, movement, rewards, and progression.
Design for latency early with prediction, interpolation, reconciliation, and clear update-rate priorities.
anti_patterns: Do not trust client-reported state for competitive or reward-bearing actions.
Do not send hidden or irrelevant entity data to clients that should not know it.
Do not add networking after gameplay systems are already tightly coupled to local state.

faq.question: Does this skill generate multiplayer server code?
faq.answer: No. It provides architecture and design guidance that can inform later implementation work.

faq.question: Which game engines does it support?
faq.answer: The guidance is engine-neutral and applies to Unity, Unreal, Godot, custom engines, and web games.

faq.question: Can it help with real-time action games?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers dedicated servers, input synchronization, prediction, interpolation, reconciliation, and lag compensation.

faq.question: Can it help with turn-based games?
faq.answer: Yes. It can recommend simpler client-server patterns and lower update requirements for turn-based gameplay.

faq.question: Does it cover anti-cheat design?
faq.answer: Yes. It emphasizes server authority, validation, hidden data control, and common cheat prevention patterns.

faq.question: Is it enough for production security?
faq.answer: No. Use it for planning, then run implementation reviews, threat modeling, and live security testing.
